fable: A man rode out one morning for the pleasure of the hunt. The chase carried him toward a patch of poor ground, where a poor man had his hut and a small field of standing grain. The deer ran into the field, and to follow it the man would have had to drive his horses through the grain and trample the crop. He pulled up at the edge. "The deer's gone into the field," said the man riding beside him. "Let it go," he answered. "I'll not ruin a poor man's crop for a morning's sport" — and he turned his horse along the edge, and took his sport another way.
moral: "One should never hurt a poor person in the pursuit of pleasure." (Knutson, trans., p. 31)

fable: A traveler came one day into a wide and sunlit land where there was no shelter anywhere, and the heat was a torment to him, the sun beating down and the bare ground scorching and cruel under it. In one place along the road certain men had gathered, whose deeds were wicked, and they had raised an awning that threw a deep and welcome shade–the one cool place in all that country. The traveler came level with them along the road. They called him to come in under their awning and shelter from the sun. But he shunned them and would not go in among them. Though the heat burnt his skin and exhausted him, he kept to the open road and left the shade behind him.
moral: "One should shun contact with wicked people, which is as terrible and threatening as the shelterless desert scorched by the rays of the summer sun." (Knutson, trans., p. 33)

fable: A man sat in his house one day, receiving those who came to him. A friend came first, and he greeted the friend kindly and spoke with him in pleasing words. After the friend left came another who was the man's enemy. The man had long been at odds with this other man, yet to this enemy he spoke just as gently and pleasantly as he had spoken to his friend, in the same welcoming and pleasing words; after a time the enemy went on his way.
moral: "One should always use pleasing language with good people and enemies alike." (Knutson, trans., p. 35)

fable: A retainer served in a great house, and in one of its affairs he knew more than his master did. One day the master spoke to him about that very matter, and had it wrong. The retainer knew well how it truly stood. He did not say, "You are mistaken, and I know better than you." He answered plainly and with respect, told his master how the matter stood, and left it there.
moral: "Even if he knows better [a good retainer] should not reply in a haughty manner." (Knutson, trans., p. 61)

fable: There was a king who had no virtue in him–neither just nor wise nor generous. A day came when calamity fell upon him. His enemies rose and overcame him, and his power and his fortune were lost. One who had served him stayed with him through it. He fell with the king, losing what the king lost, and into exile he went with him. Worthless as the king was, and fallen as he now was, the servant did not leave his side, but remained with him in the calamity.
moral: "One should never abandon a king in calamity even if he lacks all virtue." (Knutson, trans., p. 65)

fable: A great man, honored through the land, was making a long journey, and one evening he stopped at the house of an ordinary man along the road. The host took him in for the night, and with his own hands drew water for his guest, set food before him, and made ready a place for him to rest, tending to his great guest himself until morning. And this that he had done was held to be a praiseworthy thing, and those who heard of it counted it good and a cause for gladness, that he had given such service to a great man.
moral: "An act of service to a great man is always praiseworthy and a matter of rejoicing." (Knutson, trans., p. 65)

fable: A king sat in judgment, and there was brought before him a wrongdoer who had robbed and killed and done great harm among the people. The king heard the case, and when the man's guilt was plain and proven beyond doubt, the king gave a just sentence upon him. "For what this man has done, and as justice requires, let him be put to death," the king declared; and by the king's order the wrongdoer was put to death for his crimes. And in this righteous act of violence the king appeared like a great sage, as wise in his judgment as any sage in his wisdom.
moral: "When kings perform a righteous act of violence they are like great sages." (Knutson, trans., p. 77)

fable: There was a conquering king who set his heart on a neighboring territory, and he found that two other men were reaching for that same land. Thus the king marked them both as his enemies. But the two were not alike. The first, though he wanted the same land, was a lesser man. The second was the king's own equal in every virtue he himself had. The conqueror looked at the two of them, both his enemies, and knew that it was the second–the one who matched him–that he had truly to fear.
moral: "An enemy is (...) someone occupied with the same objective as the king; he is considered fearsome when he possesses the same virtues as the conqueror." (Knutson, trans., p. 97)

fable: A man had a friend of long standing, and word came to him that this friend had done him wrong. He did not cast the friend off at once on the strength of the rumor. He weighed the matter over many days and looked into it, until the friend's faults were set out plainly and shown to be true. Only then, when he had thought long and the wrong was made known beyond doubt, did he part from the friend.
moral: "Only after much deliberation should one abandon a friend, and only when his faults have been made known." (Knutson, trans., p. 109)

fable: Among a circle of friends there was one who went between them spreading rumors. To each he whispered what the others had supposedly said, and where there had been goodwill he worked to breed suspicion and quarrel. When the friends saw what he was doing and how he set them against one another, they cast him out from among them and kept his company no more.
moral: "All those who create rifts among friends should be abandoned." (Knutson, trans., p. 111)

fable: A man had charge of others' money for many years, and in all that time nothing ever went missing under his hand, so that his integrity was held to be proven. Wishing to gain riches of his own, and hearing of a king who was very rich, he set himself to win that king's trust to that end. He offered himself for the king's service and kept the royal accounts as faithfully as he had kept any other, striving all the while to gain the king's confidence so that riches might come to him by it. In time the king came to trust him and placed great wealth in his keeping, and so the man came by riches of his own.
moral: "A good retainer whose total integrity in money matters has been proven (...) should strive to win the confidence of a rich king in order to obtain riches." (Knutson, trans., p. 59)

fable: There was a king ruling over his people. A time of danger came, and he might have thrown himself recklessly into the thick of it, exposing his own body to harm. Instead he chose to guard himself and kept out of needless danger, taking care that no rash risk fell upon his person, so that his body might be preserved for the gladness and gratification of the people.
moral: "The king should protect his own body for the gratification of the people." (Knutson, trans., p. 77)

fable: A king had an enemy, and when at last he had him beaten, he destroyed him utterly and thought himself well rid of him. But no sooner was that enemy gone than another rose up in his place, as dangerous as the first. When the king had beaten this second enemy too and held him at his mercy, he did not destroy him as he had the other. Remembering how killing the first had only bred a second, he stayed his hand, made terms with the man, and took him into his own service, bringing the enemy he had defeated into the fold.
moral: "When one enemy is destroyed, another is born. Therefore never countenance the destruction of an enemy, and instead seek to bring him into the fold." (Knutson, trans., p. 107)

fable: A king had an enemy who, for all their old quarrel, could bring him great profit if the two joined together; and he had an ally of long standing who had begun to work against his interests. Thus the king made peace with the enemy and took him as a partner, since there was prosperity to be had from him. And the ally who now harmed his interests he cast off, for all their friendship, and kept him at his side no longer.
moral: "Make allies of enemies if they can contribute to your prosperity, but abandon even allies if they act against your interests." (Knutson, trans., p. 109)

fable: There was a man, and there was another who often helped him–who came to his aid in his difficulties and brought him benefit whenever there was need. Yet this other was disloyal, and the man knew him to be so. Still, because the other helped him and was of use to him, the man counted him a friend and treated him as one, for all that his loyalty was in doubt.
moral: "Whether loyal or disloyal, the one who helps you is a friend." (Knutson, trans., p. 109)

fable: There was a king who felt no fear of his enemies. Being fearless in himself, he made a great display of his power before them, showing the strength of his armies and his arms openly and without fear, so that the enemies who saw it were filled with dread of him and dared not rise against him.
moral: "The king should be fearless, provoking his enemies' fear by displays of his power, as a serpent displays its hoods." (Knutson, trans., p. 175)

fable: There was a king who was miserly and gave little away, yet he never spoke harshly to his people or frightened them with hard words; his speech to them was always gentle and pleasing, and his dealings kind. And though he was known to be miserly, the people served him willingly all the same, won over by his pleasing words and deeds.
moral: "You should not terrify people with harsh words; your speech should be pleasing. People will offer service to even a miserly king if his words and deeds are pleasing." (Knutson, trans., p. 197)

fable: There was a king who cared above all for the good of his kingdom, and bent himself to its welfare. Pleasures were offered him, and women among them, that he might give his days to indulgence. He turned away from them. He kept from that indulgence and held to the business of his realm, giving his passion to the kingdom's good and not to the vice that was set before him.
moral: "A king whose passion is the kingdom's welfare should shun the vice of women." (Knutson, trans., p. 205)

fable: A king set out to make war on an enemy and marched his army toward him to win his victory. As he went, his road carried him through a stretch of the enemy's country, and he saw that it was rich with standing crops ripe in the fields. Seeing them there in his path, he gave the order to pillage as he marched — and his army fell upon the fields, plundering and laying them waste, and carried off the harvest as the king pressed on toward his victory.
moral: "If the enemy has a territory rich in crops, the king should march to victory, pillaging the crops on his way." (Knutson, trans., p. 209)

fable: A king had an enemy whose strength lay partly in the kinsmen gathered about him. Knowing that such men, like all people, were open to the turns and discontents of fortune, the wise king set about sowing dissension among them, working quietly to turn the enemy's kinsmen against one another and against the enemy himself, so that the strength they gave him should be broken from within.
moral: "A wise king will attempt to sow dissension among his enemy’s kinsmen, since they are subject to all of life's vicissitudes." (Knutson, trans., p. 241)
